description:
What Is a Self-Funded PhD? Costs & Funding Alternatives

Direct answer box (first 50 words):

A self-funded PhD is one where you — not a university, funder or employer — pay tuition fees and living costs for three to four years. In the UK that realistically means £60,000–£100,000+ in total; in Germany or the Nordics, where PhDs are salaried jobs, self-funding is usually unnecessary.

What "self-funded" actually means

When a PhD offer or advert says "self-funded students welcome", it translates to: we will supervise you, but no money is attached. You cover two things:

  • Tuition fees, paid annually to the university — for international students in the UK commonly in the £20,000–£35,000 per year range (varies widely by university and subject; verify current fee tables)
  • Living costs, for the full duration — in the UK roughly £12,000–£15,000+ per year depending on the city, and more in London

There is no stipend, no salary, and usually no expectation that one will appear later (though some self-funded students do win funding mid-degree).

Always verify current figures officially — fees change annually. For salary-level comparison, see our PhD stipend and salary comparison by country.

Why self-funding a UK PhD is risky

Honest assessment matters here, so plainly:

  • The full cost is enormous. Six figures for a UK PhD is more than many people's graduate salary for several years.
  • Completion risk rises with money pressure. Students who must work alongside a self-funded PhD take longer and complete at lower rates.
  • "Just find funding later" rarely works. Mid-degree scholarships are rare and competitive; do not enrol on the assumption one will appear.
  • Visa financial requirements assume funding. For a UK student visa you must show maintenance funds — a self-funded route means proving that money is genuinely yours.

None of this means self-funding is always wrong. It can make sense for a short, part-time professional doctorate, or when an employer shares the cost. It is a bad default for a recent graduate.

Alternatives that cost far less

Before accepting a self-funded offer, work through these routes:

  1. Salaried PhD positions in Europe. Germany (TV-L E13 positions), the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark and Switzerland treat doctoral candidates as employees with salaries, benefits and no tuition. Competition exists, but so do far more positions than named scholarships. Our guide on how to read a PhD job advertisement shows how to check whether a post is genuinely funded and open to international candidates.
  2. Fully funded scholarships. Gates Cambridge (~£18,744 stipend plus fees — verify current figures), Rhodes (£21,060 — verify), Commonwealth, Chevening (Master's) and national schemes like DAAD (€1,400/month for doctoral students — verify on daad.de). Browse current fully funded scholarships on NextApply.
  3. UKRI-funded projects. UK doctoral training programmes and project studentships pay a tax-free stipend (recently around £19,000–£20,000 per year — verify the current rate) plus fees. You apply for a project, not for "funding" in the abstract.
  4. Structured programmes abroad. If cost is the driver, studying in Germany for free or applying to Nordic PhD posts removes the fee problem entirely rather than working around it.
  5. Employer or government sponsorship. Some employers fund doctorates tied to your role; some governments fund students who return to work at home.

If you do go self-funded: how to reduce the damage

StrategyEffect
Choose a low-fee country (Germany, Nordics)Eliminates the largest cost block entirely
Part-time PhD alongside employmentSlower, but removes the living-cost cliff
Apply to every small bursary and fee waiverRarely covers everything; shaves thousands
Negotiate fees or a studentship at year 2–3Occasionally possible; never plan around it
Secure funding before enrollingThe only strategy that genuinely removes the risk

The last row is the important one. The standard advice — and it is good advice — is: do not start a self-funded PhD in the hope of funding later. Get the funding first, then enrol.

Frequently asked questions

Is a self-funded PhD worth less than a funded one? The degree itself is identical. What differs is your experience: funded students focus on research, self-funded students often juggle work, which can affect output and completion time. Employers rarely ask how you funded it.

Can I get a scholarship after starting a self-funded PhD? Occasionally — some university bursaries, country-specific schemes and mid-degree awards exist — but they are scarce and competitive. Never enrol on this hope.

Do UK universities offer funding to international PhD students? Yes, through UKRI studentships, university scholarships and project funding, but international-eligible places are limited and very competitive. Apply early in the cycle and treat self-funding as the fallback, not the plan.

Which countries pay PhD students a salary? Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Switzerland all offer salaried doctoral positions in most fields. Check whether the position requires a Master's first — many do.

Official source

Fee levels, stipend rates and visa financial requirements change every year. Verify current figures on the official university and government pages (UKRI, UKVI, DAAD, university fee tables) before making any decision based on the numbers in this article.
